findings.description: The judge binding (grader 1.5.0) identifies a judged finding only by {file, anchor_line[, anchor_line_end]} and the run id. finding_sha256 is the RFC 8785 hash of that reference, so it does not cover the finding's text (title/description/scenario) that the judge actually read, nor any hash of the run's findings output. judge_setup (line 3710) defaults run_id to the run or cell directory's basename, which is not unique across arms or cells (e.g. two `r1` directories under different arms). Consequently a `describes` verdict issued for one finding remains valid for (a) a different finding text later written at the same file:line of the same run directory and (b) any other run whose directory has the same basename and cites the same file:line for the same defect. The stale-verdict checks (grader_version, fixture_sha256, pair membership, finding_sha256) all pass in both cases, so recall_judged is computed from a verdict about text that was never judged.
findings.failure_mode: When a run directory's findings file is edited after judging, or when verdict rows are aggregated across runs that share a directory basename and the operator relies on the default run id, then verdicts transfer to un-judged finding text and recall_judged is reported as if those pairs had been judged.
findings.suggested_fix: Include a content hash in the reference (e.g. sha256 of the citation's source bullet or of the combined findings artefact) in finding_sha256, record a findings_sha256 of the run output in the judge block, and either require --run-id explicitly or derive the default from a content hash rather than the directory basename. Reject a grade whose current findings hash differs from the one the verdict rows name.
findings.failure_scenario: When a run directory's findings file is edited after judging, or when verdict rows are aggregated across runs that share a directory basename and the operator relies on the default run id, then verdicts transfer to un-judged finding text and recall_judged is reported as if those pairs had been judged.

findings.cross_file_justification: write_tasks is the shared sink now called by seed-corpus-from-external.sh (diff-touched, truncated from this review), which seeds from a hostile public repository; the value of `what` passed by that caller could not be inspected here.
findings.description: write_tasks interpolates `what` unescaped into a double-quoted YAML scalar (`description: "{verb} {what}"`) and writes the result as a task.yaml. `fx` is validated elsewhere and `tags` go through json.dumps, but `what` has no escaping: a double quote, backslash or newline terminates the scalar and lets the remainder be parsed as further YAML keys of the task document. If the external seeder derives `what` from repository-controlled text (PR title, repository description), a hostile repository can shape the task definition that the harness later executes (prompt, grader script name, timeouts) or at minimum make the task unparseable. Whether duplicate keys win or error depends on the YAML parser used by the harness, so the effect ranges from a broken task to a modified one.
findings.failure_mode: When the external seeder passes repository-derived text as `what` and that text contains a double quote or newline, then the generated task.yaml contains attacker-shaped keys (prompt, graders) or fails to parse, and the operator may commit it unnoticed because the labels approval covers the manifest rather than the task file.
findings.suggested_fix: Emit the description with json.dumps(f"{verb} {what}") (JSON strings are valid YAML double-quoted scalars) or build the task with a YAML emitter; additionally pass `what` through clean() and reject control characters before writing.
findings.failure_scenario: When the external seeder passes repository-derived text as `what` and that text contains a double quote or newline, then the generated task.yaml contains attacker-shaped keys (prompt, graders) or fails to parse, and the operator may commit it unnoticed because the labels approval covers the manifest rather than the task file.

findings.cross_file_justification: The (path, bytes) lists come from the two seeders (seed-corpus-from-record.sh and the new seed-corpus-from-external.sh, both diff-touched and truncated here). The external seeder's unsafe-path refusal is described in the reviewer context but the sink itself performs no check, so a validation gap or a future third caller writes outside the fixture directory.
findings.description: write_layout computes `dest = os.path.join(fdir, sub, rel)` and writes each entry with makedirs + open("wb") without validating `rel`. os.path.join discards everything before an absolute component, and `..` components are honoured by the kernel at open time, so an entry such as `/x`, `../x` or `a/../../x` writes outside `<fixture>/base` or `<fixture>/head`. Tree entries of a hostile repository are attacker-controlled (git only refuses such names at checkout, not in trees returned by ls-tree or the trees API). head_path() in the same library already implements the right check for labels files, but write_layout does not reuse it. The function also does not guard against an entry named like an existing directory or a case-folding collision on case-insensitive filesystems, which silently drops files from the fixture.
findings.failure_mode: When a seeder passes a tree entry whose path is absolute or contains a `..` component and the caller's own refusal misses it, then write_layout creates files outside the --out fixture directory on the operator's machine with repository-controlled content.
findings.suggested_fix: Validate every `rel` inside write_layout with the same rule as head_path (reject empty, absolute, backslash, NUL, `..` or `.` segments; confirm os.path.realpath(dest) stays under the sub-directory) and fail the seed on the first offender; apply the check to both base_files and head_files.
findings.failure_scenario: When a seeder passes a tree entry whose path is absolute or contains a `..` component and the caller's own refusal misses it, then write_layout creates files outside the --out fixture directory on the operator's machine with repository-controlled content.

findings.description: floor_amendments lets one floor file differ from origin/main when its bytes hash to the pinned sha256, the change is additive (no deleted lines) and a DEC id is named. For shell scripts the additive-only rule is not a weakening-prevention property: inserted lines can `exit 0`/`return 0` before the enforcing code, redefine a function later in the file (bash keeps the last definition), add a `trap` or an early `[[ -n $KNOB ]] && exit 0` escape, all with zero deleted lines. The protective pin on floor.yaml itself (FLOOR_SHA256 in the bats suites) is updated by the same actor adding the row, and `authority` is free text unless the test resolves it against a decisions ledger (not visible in this review). The current row is for verdict-derive.sh, but the schema accepts any floor file including adversarial-review-gate.sh and settings.deny.json.
findings.failure_mode: When an actor with branch write access adds an amendment row for adversarial-review-gate.sh, bumps FLOOR_SHA256 and inserts an early exit into the gate without deleting lines, then floor-snapshot.bats passes and the review gate is bypassed for the rest of the cycle while the floor reports intact.
findings.suggested_fix: Restrict amendments to non-executable floor files, or require the row to pin both the origin/main base sha and a reviewed diff hash and verify `authority` against the tracked decisions ledger; additionally reject amendments for files listed under floor_guards' gate scripts unless a second DEC co-signs, and assert the file still passes its own guard unit tests at the amended sha.
findings.failure_scenario: When an actor with branch write access adds an amendment row for adversarial-review-gate.sh, bumps FLOOR_SHA256 and inserts an early exit into the gate without deleting lines, then floor-snapshot.bats passes and the review gate is bypassed for the rest of the cycle while the floor reports intact.

findings.description: The comment above SECRET_RX states that patterns stay on one line so a redaction never joins lines, and redact()'s docstring says line numbers never move. The PEM pattern `-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----[^-]*-----END ...` uses `[^-]*`, which matches newlines, so a multi-line key block collapses to a single REDACTED-TEST-SECRET token in base/, head/ and head.diff. Lines after the block shift, head.diff hunk counts no longer match the files, and fix regions (`fix/<sha>:<start>-<end>`, taken from the original commit) point at the wrong lines. Labels anchors resolved against the redacted head stay self-consistent, so the impact is a corrupted fixture rather than exposure.
findings.failure_mode: When a seeded repository contains a multi-line test private key in a reviewed file, then redaction shifts every later line of that file and head.diff, misaligning fix regions and the ±3 crediting window for defects below the block.
findings.suggested_fix: Redact PEM blocks line by line (replace each inner line with the marker and keep the line count), or match `[^\n-]*` per line and leave the BEGIN/END lines in place; add a test asserting line counts are unchanged after redact().
findings.failure_scenario: When a seeded repository contains a multi-line test private key in a reviewed file, then redaction shifts every later line of that file and head.diff, misaligning fix regions and the ±3 crediting window for defects below the block.

findings.description: linger_ok now reads the cgroup file from LOA_SUPERVISOR_CGROUP_FILE. The knob is intended for bats but is honoured unconditionally, so any environment that sets it to a file containing `/system.slice/` bypasses the linger precondition in production, allowing a detached batch to be started where it will be killed at logout. The sibling knob LOA_SUPERVISOR_BOOT_ID_FILE has the same shape.
findings.failure_mode: When an operator's environment or a wrapper exports LOA_SUPERVISOR_CGROUP_FILE pointing at a file with a system.slice path, then the supervisor skips the linger check and a long-running batch dies silently at session logout.
findings.suggested_fix: Gate the override on the existing test guard pattern used elsewhere in the harness (BATS_TEST_FILENAME set and LOA_EGRESS_TEST_MODE-style flag), or ignore the knob unless the path is under $BATS_TEST_TMPDIR.
findings.failure_scenario: When an operator's environment or a wrapper exports LOA_SUPERVISOR_CGROUP_FILE pointing at a file with a system.slice path, then the supervisor skips the linger check and a long-running batch dies silently at session logout.

findings.description: The sandbox now runs with `--network container:<guard>` and relies on netfilter rules installed in the guard's namespace (NET_ADMIN, then privilege drop). Because the namespace is shared, the rules are only as strong as the sandbox container's own capability set: a sandbox process holding CAP_NET_ADMIN in the init user namespace could alter them. The visible part of the sandbox `docker run` sets `--user` but the capability flags are outside the reviewed hunk, and cmd_guard does not assert anything about the joining container. Secondary: the shared namespace exposes Docker's embedded DNS, which resolves the names of every container on the batch network (other sessions' guard names embed their CUR_NAME), a minor cross-session information leak.
findings.failure_mode: When the sandbox container is started without `--cap-drop ALL` (or with NET_ADMIN re-added by a profile), then a process inside the sandbox can flush the guard's rules and reach the host gateway or other containers despite egress.json recording enforced: true.
findings.suggested_fix: Confirm the sandbox run line uses `--cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges` on both launchers and record that in egress.json; have the guard entrypoint also install rules in a way that requires NET_ADMIN to undo and have self-check attempt a rule flush from the probe container to prove it fails.
findings.failure_scenario: When the sandbox container is started without `--cap-drop ALL` (or with NET_ADMIN re-added by a profile), then a process inside the sandbox can flush the guard's rules and reach the host gateway or other containers despite egress.json recording enforced: true.

findings.description: The verdict rows' provenance fields (blind, judge_model, judge_prompt_sha256, ts) are self-asserted with no signature or external check, yet `blind` decides which verdicts enter recall_judged. grade.json records only effective verdicts plus a count of superseded rows, not the superseded chain, and a row that became stale (key or grader change) must be deleted rather than superseded because every row of this run is validated first. The file's history is therefore lossy and the only tamper evidence is verdicts_sha256, which lives in the same grade.json a later actor would regenerate.
findings.failure_mode: When a verdict file is rewritten after the fact (rows deleted, blind flipped to true, stale rows removed) and the grade is re-run, then grade.json shows a clean effective set with no record of what was previously judged.
findings.suggested_fix: Record the superseded rows (hash, line, verdict) in the judge block, allow superseding a stale row so history is kept, and consider an append-only verdicts ledger whose head hash is stored outside the run directory (or signed by the judge process).
findings.failure_scenario: When a verdict file is rewritten after the fact (rows deleted, blind flipped to true, stale rows removed) and the grade is re-run, then grade.json shows a clean effective set with no record of what was previously judged.
